chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
title: Bringing his brother-in-law Russell Bowles into Lunceford's band
summary: Lunceford refused New York players like Dickie Wells but let Jones's brother-in-law sit in on New Year's Eve and kept him until the band broke up.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: So I remember once when he needed a trombone player, he was going to try a trombone player, so right away I said Dickie Wells. So he said, "No, I don't want no New York musicians. I have to get somebody else, you know." You know, it was funny about that, he'd always send somewhere
else, you know, like we brought in Jock Carruthers, you know, sent to Kansas City and brought him in.
Well, maybe he thought they'd be a little too hip to work like that.
Yeah, I think that was it.

But anyhow, I said, 'Well, what about my brother-in-law, Russell?' You know, so he said, 'Have him to come down. I've got a gig New Years Eve, and have him to come down and sit in.' So he come down and sat in, so he kept him, you know.
Oh. How long did Russell stay with the band?
Yeah. When it broke up he went down to Macy's and got him a job.
He was happy in the band, huh?
Yeah, he must have been, yeah. But he never was the type of guy -- he's the type of guy that just liked whatever happened, you know.
But I mean he didn't play a lot of get-off, did he?
No, he didn't play too much. But he knew a little bit, because he followed Dicky and his band back in

Kentucky before he left, and he was playing things like, "What You Call Them Blues," and, "Stampede," and all that stuff. You know, they'd take them off of records, you know. So I imagine he must have took the solos off too.
